segments.script: First, meaning. I read “My children, ye will lose your sire today, / For all of me has perished, and no more / Have ye to bear your long, long ministry; / A heavy load, I know, and yet one word / Wipes out all score of tribulations—love. / And love from me ye had—from no man more; / But now must live without me all your days.” slowly and put it in my own words: The Messenger repeats Oedipus' farewell: his daughters will lose their father today, their long care for him is over, and one word, love, outweighs all their burdens. Next, craft. I notice the heavy load is set against a single word placed at the end of the line, love, which is then repeated. The strongest word is “love”: his last word to his daughters. Then, effect. Why does Oedipus end his farewell with the word love? My answer: Oedipus ends his farewell with the word love because it is the one thing that repays his daughters' long service; the cursed king's last gift is not power or a curse but love.

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The cursed man becomes a protector of the city. His last word to his daughters is "love" (line 1661). Useful evidence: “It was a messenger from heaven, or else / Some gentle, painless cleaving of earth’s base; / For without wailing or disease or pain / He passed away—an end most marvellous” (Exodos (lines 1626–1831), Messenger): Messenger, lines 1702–1705. On theme: A messenger reports Oedipus' last farewell and his mysterious passing, seen only by Theseus. The daughters mourn. Theseus keeps his promise not to reveal the grave and promises them his care. Antigone resolves to return to Thebes. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
